cards.title: Redstart Travel
facts: Redstarts are small migratory birds that travel up to 1 km in altitude during their seasonal migrations.
These birds are known for their distinctive red tail feathers and are found across Europe and Asia.

cards.title: Crane Travel
facts: Cranes are large birds that can fly at altitudes of up to 2 km during migration.
They are known for their elaborate courtship dances and can live for over 20 years in the wild.

cards.title: Hot Air Balloon (Typical)
facts: Hot air balloons typically operate at altitudes of 3 km, providing spectacular views of the landscape below.
The first manned hot air balloon flight was conducted by the Montgolfier brothers in 1783 in France.

cards.title: Altocumulus Clouds
facts: Altocumulus clouds form at mid-level altitudes around 4.5 km and are composed of water droplets.
These clouds often indicate atmospheric instability and can precede thunderstorms.

cards.title: Biplane (Typical)
facts: Early biplanes typically operated at altitudes of 5.5 km, with the world altitude record for biplanes reaching over 8 km.
Biplanes were the dominant aircraft design during World War I due to their superior maneuverability.

sources.label: Smithsonian National Air and Space Museum

cards.title: Nimbostratus Clouds
facts: Nimbostratus clouds form at low to mid-levels around 5 km and produce steady precipitation.
These clouds are typically dark gray and cover large areas of the sky.

cards.title: Vulture (Maximum)
facts: Rüppell's vulture holds the record for the highest flying bird, reaching altitudes of 11.9 km.
These vultures have specialized hemoglobin that allows them to function at extreme altitudes with low oxygen levels.

cards.title: Boeing 747 Travel Height
facts: The Boeing 747 typically cruises at altitudes of 12 km, where the air is thin and fuel efficiency is optimized.
At this altitude, passengers experience reduced atmospheric pressure, equivalent to being at 2,400 meters above sea level.

cards.title: Cumulonimbus Clouds (Maximum)
facts: Cumulonimbus clouds can reach heights of 13 km, forming the tallest cloud structures on Earth.
These clouds are associated with severe weather including thunderstorms, hail, and tornadoes.

cards.title: Troposphere (Maximum)
facts: The troposphere extends up to 15 km and contains 75% of the atmosphere's mass and 99% of its water vapor.
This is where most weather phenomena occur, including clouds, precipitation, and storms.

cards.title: Biplane (Maximum)
facts: The highest altitude achieved by a biplane was 17 km, demonstrating the remarkable capabilities of early aviation.
This record was set in the 1930s when aviation technology was rapidly advancing.

cards.title: Glider (Typical)
facts: Gliders typically operate at altitudes of 2.5 km, using thermal updrafts to maintain flight.
Modern gliders can stay airborne for hours by exploiting rising air currents and weather patterns.

cards.title: Glider (Maximum)
facts: The highest altitude achieved by a glider is 23 km, set by Perlan Project's pressurized glider.
This altitude is in the stratosphere, where gliders can ride mountain wave systems for extended flights.

cards.title: Lockheed U-2
facts: The Lockheed U-2 spy plane operates at altitudes of 21 km, above most commercial air traffic.
This high-altitude reconnaissance aircraft has been in service since 1956 and can stay airborne for over 12 hours.

cards.title: Hot Air Balloon (Maximum)
facts: The highest altitude achieved by a hot air balloon is 21 km, set by Vijaypat Singhania in 2005.
At this altitude, the balloon operates in the stratosphere where atmospheric pressure is extremely low.

cards.title: Lockheed SR-71
facts: The SR-71 Blackbird could reach altitudes of 26 km, making it one of the highest-flying aircraft ever built.
This reconnaissance aircraft could fly at speeds exceeding Mach 3 and was virtually untouchable by enemy defenses.

sources.label: National Museum of the US Air Force

cards.title: Red Bull Stratos Balloon
facts: The Red Bull Stratos mission reached 39 km altitude, where Felix Baumgartner performed a record-breaking freefall.
At this altitude, the atmospheric pressure is less than 1% of sea level, requiring specialized life support systems.

cards.title: Ozone Layer
facts: The ozone layer is concentrated at 22 km altitude and protects Earth from harmful ultraviolet radiation.
This protective layer absorbs 97-99% of the Sun's high-frequency ultraviolet light, making life on Earth possible.

cards.title: Stratosphere (Maximum)
facts: The stratosphere extends up to 50 km and contains the ozone layer that protects Earth from UV radiation.
This atmospheric layer is characterized by increasing temperature with altitude, unlike the troposphere below.

cards.title: Mesosphere (Maximum)
facts: The mesosphere extends up to 85 km and is where most meteors burn up upon entering Earth's atmosphere.
This layer has the coldest temperatures in the atmosphere, dropping to as low as -90°C.

cards.title: Shooting Star
facts: Shooting stars (meteors) typically burn up at 95 km altitude, creating the spectacular light shows we see.
These meteors are usually no larger than a grain of sand but can create brilliant streaks of light as they vaporize.

cards.title: Thermosphere (Maximum)
facts: The thermosphere extends up to 600 km and is where the International Space Station orbits.
This layer experiences extreme temperature variations, from -90°C to over 2000°C depending on solar activity.

cards.title: Sputnik
facts: Sputnik 1, the first artificial satellite, orbited Earth at 939 km altitude in 1957.
This historic satellite marked the beginning of the Space Age and the start of the space race between the US and USSR.

cards.title: International Space Station
facts: The ISS orbits Earth at 420 km altitude, completing one orbit every 90 minutes.
This multinational space station has been continuously occupied since 2000 and serves as a microgravity laboratory.

cards.title: Hubble Space Telescope
facts: The Hubble Space Telescope orbits at 540 km altitude, above Earth's atmosphere for clear astronomical observations.
Since its launch in 1990, Hubble has revolutionized our understanding of the universe with over 1.5 million observations.

cards.title: Mir Space Station
facts: The Mir space station operated at 400 km altitude from 1986 to 2001, setting records for continuous human presence in space.
This Soviet space station was the first modular space station and served as a precursor to the International Space Station.

cards.title: Starlink Satellite
facts: Starlink satellites operate at 550 km altitude, providing global internet coverage from low Earth orbit.
This constellation of thousands of satellites aims to bring high-speed internet to remote areas worldwide.

cards.title: EnMAP Satellite
facts: The EnMAP (Environmental Mapping and Analysis Program) satellite operates at 650 km altitude for Earth observation.
This German satellite provides hyperspectral imaging data for environmental monitoring and scientific research.

cards.title: GPS Satellites
facts: GPS satellites orbit at 20,200 km altitude, providing global positioning and navigation services.
The GPS constellation consists of 24 active satellites that enable precise location tracking worldwide.

cards.title: Meteosat
facts: Meteosat weather satellites operate at 36,000 km altitude in geostationary orbit.
These satellites provide continuous weather monitoring and forecasting for Europe and Africa.

cards.title: Astra Satellite
facts: Astra satellites operate at 35,786 km altitude in geostationary orbit for telecommunications.
This altitude allows satellites to maintain a fixed position relative to Earth's surface.

cards.title: Moon
facts: The Moon orbits Earth at an average distance of 384,000 km, making it our closest celestial neighbor.
This distance is equivalent to about 30 Earth diameters, and light takes 1.3 seconds to travel from Moon to Earth.

cards.title: Mercury
facts: Mercury is the closest planet to the Sun, with an average distance of 222 million km from Earth.
Despite being the smallest planet, Mercury has extreme temperature variations from 427°C to -173°C.

cards.title: Venus
facts: Venus is the second planet from the Sun, with an average distance of 261 million km from Earth.
Known as Earth's twin, Venus has a thick atmosphere of carbon dioxide and surface temperatures hot enough to melt lead.

cards.title: Mars
facts: Mars, the Red Planet, has an average distance of 401 million km from Earth.
Mars has the largest volcano in the solar system (Olympus Mons) and evidence suggests it once had liquid water on its surface.

cards.title: Jupiter
facts: Jupiter, the largest planet in our solar system, has an average distance of 968 million km from Earth.
This gas giant has over 80 moons and a Great Red Spot storm that has been raging for centuries.

cards.title: Saturn
facts: Saturn, famous for its rings, has an average distance of 1.66 billion km from Earth.
This gas giant is less dense than water and has over 80 moons, including the massive Titan.

cards.title: Uranus
facts: Uranus, the ice giant, has an average distance of 3.1 billion km from Earth.
This planet rotates on its side and has faint rings and 27 known moons.

cards.title: Neptune
facts: Neptune, the farthest planet from the Sun, has an average distance of 4.6 billion km from Earth.
This ice giant has the strongest winds in the solar system, reaching speeds of 2,100 km/h.

cards.title: Pluto
facts: Pluto, now classified as a dwarf planet, has an average distance of 7.5 billion km from Earth.
This distant world has a heart-shaped glacier and five moons, including the largest, Charon.

cards.title: Ceres
facts: Ceres, the largest object in the asteroid belt, has an average distance of 450 million km from Earth.
This dwarf planet contains more fresh water than Earth and may have a subsurface ocean.

cards.title: Comet Halley
facts: Halley's Comet has an average distance of 5.3 billion km from Earth and returns every 76 years.
This famous comet was last seen in 1986 and will next appear in 2061, leaving a trail of debris that creates meteor showers.

cards.title: Voyager 1
facts: Voyager 1 is currently 24 billion km from Earth, making it the farthest human-made object in space.
Launched in 1977, this spacecraft has entered interstellar space and continues to send data back to Earth.

cards.title: James Webb Space Telescope
facts: The James Webb Space Telescope operates at 1.5 million km from Earth at the L2 Lagrange point.
This revolutionary telescope can see the first galaxies that formed after the Big Bang and study exoplanet atmospheres.

cards.title: Exosphere Geocorona
facts: The exosphere extends up to 10,000 km and is the outermost layer of Earth's atmosphere.
This region contains the geocorona, a cloud of hydrogen atoms that extends far into space.

cards.title: Polar Lights (Aurora)
facts: Polar lights (aurora) occur at altitudes of 150 km when charged particles from the Sun interact with Earth's magnetic field.
These spectacular light displays are most commonly seen near the polar regions and are caused by solar wind particles.

cards.title: Volcano Ash Cloud
facts: Volcanic ash clouds can reach altitudes of 57 km, affecting global climate and aviation.
The 1991 Mount Pinatubo eruption injected ash and sulfur dioxide into the stratosphere, causing global temperature drops.

cards.title: Cirrus Clouds
facts: Cirrus clouds form at altitudes of 9 km and are composed of ice crystals.
These wispy, high-altitude clouds are often indicators of approaching weather changes.

cards.title: Stratocumulus Clouds
facts: Stratocumulus clouds form at low altitudes of 1.5 km and often cover large areas of the sky.
These clouds are associated with stable weather conditions and can persist for long periods.
